label: November 1880–December 1882
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 861 episodes reported from November 1880 through December 1882, in one list: 64 from November–December 1880 (38 on the map); 433 from January–December 1881 (257 on the map); 364 from January–December 1882 (202 on the map). The map shows the 497 episodes that involve anti-Black violence or threats, month by month across the years. Each collection’s own notes on scope, sources and method follow.

January–December 1882

Dossiers for 364 episodes reported from January through December 1882. Like 1881, this collection covers two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white, Mexican and Native American victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers; only the anti-Black episodes are on the map. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later, and from searches for victims in the Beck–Tolnay and Monroe Work Today inventories that the month runs missed. The search used white papers only. Events from December 1881 first reported in these months were moved to the 1881 collection.

We wrote 414 dossiers; 50 are set aside, and 195 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope or already in 1881. Set aside: 6 duplicates; reports that proved false, hypothetical or about an earlier year; one event that took place in Canada; and events with no force, no race given, no Black target, or no racial element outside a lynching.

Inventory differences are kept and noted, not counted. Beck–Tolnay lists James M. Davis, a revenue officer ambushed by moonshiners near McMinnville, Tennessee, in March, as lynched; our papers describe an ambush of an officer, which our rules do not count as a lynching. Calvin Luckey’s lynching in Randolph County, West Virginia, is counted as probable: local papers denied it.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals. An attack by one private person counts when it has racial content or context, such as a whipping over an alleged insult to a white woman or an ambush of Black families; a quarrel that happens to cross the color line is set aside.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom, and what the reports suggest lay behind a killing; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.

January–December 1881

Dossiers for 433 episodes reported from January through December 1881. These months cover two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white, Mexican, Italian and Chinese victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are therefore included here, unlike in our other months. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later; from the Monroe Work Today inventory, our only lynching list for this year; and from a check for attacks by one person (a separate pass over every article for July and August, part of the first screen for January through June). Each month’s search also read the following month’s papers for more on known episodes, and December’s read January 1882. For 1881 the search used white papers only. January also holds events from late December 1880 that were first reported in January; they are marked as falling before the year. Older 1880 events that 1881 papers recalled, among them testimony on violence at the November 1880 election, are held for a separate 1880 collection.

We wrote 528 dossiers; 95 are set aside, and 32 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope. Set aside: twenty-six duplicates; four events from other months; anti-Black-scope events in which no report gives anyone’s race and no lynching was involved (twenty); events with no force, two-sided fights, a killing with no Black victim, reports a contemporary source denied, rumors and forecasts of lynchings where no crowd gathered, threatened lynchings of Black prisoners by Black crowds, an attempt to free two prisoners from a jail, and joke items from Tombstone, Deadwood and Kentucky.

Some episodes run over several days and towns. Where a pursuit moved from one jail to another, as with John Taylor in North Carolina in June, each raid is its own entry and the entries link to one another; the victim is counted once, at the lynching.

Inventory differences are kept and noted, not counted: Perry Thompson in Sharkey County, Mississippi, whom the inventory lists as lynched and the papers describe as killed when hidden men fired on Black men walking to a political meeting; and Juarique and Sanchez near El Paso in April, whom the inventory lists as lynched and the papers describe as shot by Americans in a quarrel over land. The inventory’s thirteen victims at Las Animas are set aside: the papers place a robbery ambush of Mexican traders in Sonora, Mexico.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals; manhunts for an accused Black man with no capture reported are kept as an upper bound. Peonage, force used to hold a Black worker to labor, is always included. An attack by one private person counts when it has racial content or context, such as a whipping over an alleged insult to a white woman or an ambush of Black families; a quarrel that happens to cross the color line is set aside.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.

November–December 1880

Dossiers for 64 episodes reported from November through December 1880. As in 1881 and 1882, this collection covers two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white victims and others, and the many lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers; only the anti-Black episodes are on the map. November opened with the presidential election, and much of the month’s violence came with it: Red Shirts holding the polls at Darlington, South Carolina, at gunpoint, election-day riots at Edgefield, Johnston and Sumter, and Black voters driven from the polls. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later, and from searches for victims in the Monroe Work Today inventory that the month runs missed. The search used white papers only: American Stories and the other Chronicling America pages, and, new with these months, pages from four state digital-newspaper programs (Georgia, Pennsylvania, Nebraska and Oregon) that neither holds. These pages, most of them Georgia papers such as the Savannah Morning News and the Columbus dailies, added six episodes and new reports of eleven others. The rest of 1880, January to October, is still to come; the July and August 1880 dossiers from our August series will join this collection when those months are run.

We wrote 82 dossiers; 18 are set aside, and 21 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope. Set aside: four duplicates; a November report recalling two lynchings from earlier in 1880, held for those months; anti-Black-scope events in which no report gives anyone’s race and no lynching was involved (eight); an event with no force; a night shooting by one man with no racial element found; a cannon said to have been aimed at voters, reported only as hearsay; and a threatened lynching of a Black man by a Black crowd.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals. An attack by one private person counts when it has racial content or context, such as a whipping over an alleged insult to a white woman or an ambush of Black families; a quarrel that happens to cross the color line is set aside.

Method: a research agent searched the papers; for these months it was OpenAI’s Codex or Google’s Gemini. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom, and what the reports suggest lay behind a killing; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.
